data.title: Dolné Orešany – Vápenice, or how we found a new hillfort
data.excerpt: In the summer of 2017, two members of the Hradiská civic association set out to look for the spot in the Majdán area where a hoard of Celtic coins may have been found. Instead they climbed a low hill with very steep slopes and found prehistoric sherds on its summit plateau – a site unknown until then, from which the subsequent excavation brought an iron spearhead, an arrowhead, part of a spur and a gold (electrum) wire.

data.metaDescription: The story of the 2017 discovery of the Vápenice upland site near Dolné Orešany: an iron spearhead, a spur and a gold wire from a hill guarded by a palisade.

children.text: In the summer of 2017, together with another member of our association, Lukáš Ilavský, I was roaming the sites we had selected in the surroundings of Majdán (between Horné and Dolné Orešany). Our aim was to try to find the place where a hoard of Celtic coins may have been found, which had been published in the specialist literature shortly before. The article by Mr Frohlich gives only Majdán in general terms, which is, however, a fairly broad notion. We selected several sites, focusing of course on hills and spurs which, judging by the map, might have been suitable as upland sites and hillforts. In doing so we tried to discover possible fortifications, or sherd material that would demonstrate occupation of such a site.

blocks.alt: Dolné Orešany – Vápenice (or how we found a new hillfort)

children.text: One day our efforts were crowned with success. We scrambled up a hill that was admittedly not very high, but was protected by steep to vertical slopes and looked promising on the map. It lay essentially right opposite the site known as Husí Stok, where water rises. Already during our climb to the top of the hill my attention was caught by a prehistoric sherd. Once we had reached the summit plateau we found such sherds in abundance. At that moment it was clear to us that this little hill had been inhabited in ancient times! It was an enormous joy. We recorded the positions of several sherds and took them with us, and then showed and handed them over to the archaeologists Matúš Sládok (the Regional Monuments Board in Trnava) and Pavol Jelínek (the Slovak National Museum in Bratislava). After going through the available databases, they established that this was a site unknown until then! Our joy was therefore even greater.

An archaeological excavation was then authorised at the site by a decision of the Regional Monuments Board in Trnava and carried out by the Slovak National Museum in Bratislava. For understandable reasons our Hradiská civic association also took part in the excavation, armed with great expectations and metal detectors. Fortune smiled on me first, when an evidently large piece of iron rang out under my detector. To our enormous delight, a large iron spearhead emerged from under the ground! Shortly afterwards another of our members had reason to rejoice – Lukáš Ilavský, who found a beautiful iron arrowhead. Other interesting finds from the site were part of an iron spur, a fire-steel and a spherical button. The greatest masterstroke, however, was achieved by Lukáš Kotásek, who dug up a gold – more precisely electrum – wire at the site! His joyful cry, and then ours, carried out across the whole of Orešany! With our finds we thus enriched the history of Dolné Orešany. Every find, together with the circumstances of its discovery, was carefully documented by Pavol Jelínek, archaeologist of the Slovak National Museum. He recorded above all the position, depth and orientation of each find and other important details.

blocks.alt: Dolné Orešany – Vápenice (or how we found a new hillfort)

children.text: These finds, together with a quantity of sherd material, confirmed that Vápenica was used in the past by our ancestors as an upland site. We did not manage to identify any rampart defences, and I therefore conclude that the hill may have been protected only by a timber palisade. Given the steepness of its slopes, this possibility appears essentially sufficient. The article briefly summarising the results of this excavation of ours forms part of our edited volume on hillforts (
Hradiská – Svedkovia dávnych čias 2 (Hillforts – Witnesses of Ancient Times 2)

). We are very glad that our association took part in this way, together with the Regional Monuments Board in Trnava and the Slovak National Museum in Bratislava, in saving our archaeological heritage. Our great thanks therefore also go to the Regional Monuments Board in Trnava and the Slovak National Museum in Bratislava for organising the rescue excavation so quickly and flexibly, and one that brought excellent results as well.
